nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
01/06/94. R. E. Braun | R. G. Gilmore; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

FLELMR CODE: 1948

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Clown Goby
Scientific Name: Microgobius gulosus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
Class: Osteichthyes
Order: Perciformes
Family: Gobiidae

nodes.title: Other Common Names
nodes.body:
Note:	Reference for Scientific Name (Girard 1858)
	Reference for Classification (956)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: None
Recreational: None
Ecological Role:  The clown goby is found commonly in a wide variety of habitats, including seagrass meadows, mangroves, open bottoms, marsh ponds, canals and fresh water tributaries (1141; 887; 848, 948, 993; 1242). Odum and Heald (1972) found that Lutjanus griseus feeds on this species. A variety of other sparids, sciaenids, lutjanids, flatfish and barracuda, among others, consume various gobiid species (163; 664; 702; 1016; 934; 672; 982). Because of the abundance and consumption by a wide variety of predators, gobies undoubtedly play an important trophic role in most low latitude estuaries.
Indicator: This species has been considered as an indicator of environmental impacts caused by shuttle launches at the Kennedy Space Center (1214). It was chosen for evaluation as an indicator because it occupies the consumer level in the aquatic food web. As such, it would be directly and indirectly affected by chemical and physical changes in the environment, such as ephemeral drops in pH (to 1.5) as a result of shuttle launches (1214).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The clown goby is found along the Atlantic coast and the Gulf of Mexico from Chesapeake Bay to Colpus Christi, Texas, including Lake Okeechobee, Florida (1116; 632; 1090; 790).
Within Study Area: This goby is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon and its freshwater tributaries (1141; 887; 848, 1987, 1988; 1242; 1187).
Movements and Migrations: This species is a year round resident of shallow fringing habitats within the Indian River Lagoon (Gilmore unpub. data).
Life Mode: The clown goby is a euryhaline, epibenthic, opportunistic carnivore found in a wide variety of habitats, a truly euryoecious species (1086; 887; 848; 790; 1214). This species is sexually dimorphic and displays territorial behavior (1141; 1086).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body: This goby is found in a variety of habitats, including seagrass meadows, mangroves, open bottoms, marsh ponds, canals and fresh water tributaries (1141; 887; 848, 1987. 1988; 1242). Dawson (1969), in work from the Gulf of Mexico, states that "this species occurs most frequently in muddy, estuarine localities and in habitats protected by aquatic vegetation." In the Indian River Lagoon, clown gobies are not found near ocean inlets but are common in quite protected habitats with low hydrological energy (887; 848, 1988; 1098; 1214).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
This species is usually collected over soft sand, silt or muddy bottoms sometimes associated with seagrass, mangroves, or freshwater tributaries (1141, 1116, 848, 1988; 1242; 790; 1214)
Physical/Chemical:  The clown goby has been collected in Florida from waters with a temperature range of 12.0 to 34.1 OC and a salinity range of 0.0 to 36.6 ppt (664; 887; 885).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Clown gobies are gonochoristic, oviparous, and sexual dimorphic. Provancha and Hall (1991) suggest that species with low fecundity such as clown goby may exhibit some parental care. This has been observed in the related species, Gobiosoma bosc by Dahlberg and Conyers (1973), Mok (1981) and others and is typical of gobiid fishes (Breder and Rosen 1966; Thresher 1984).
Mating/Spawning: Provancha and Hall (1991) found that in the northern Indian River Lagoon this goby spawns over a protracted period with young of the year appearing in May. Gonadosomatic index was highest in March and April prior to the onset of spawning. Spawning continued until late fall. Populations from other locations may however spawn all year round as indicated by observations made by Springer and Woodburn (1960). They collected ripe females in July and November in Tampa Bay. Gilmore (unpub. data) has collected individuals less than 15 mm SL from the southern Indian River Lagoon in January, March, May, July, September, October and November.
Fecundity: The mean number of ova was low with 305 + 77.5 eggs found in 25 gravid females from 35 to 49 mm (1214).

nodes.title: GROWTH
nodes.body:
Egg: Provancha and Hall (1991) found eggs that were "a dark golden color and well developed" in 4 gravid females (41 to 49 ~nm). These eggs had a total mean diameter of 0.66 + 0.21 mm.  The largest egg examined was 1.14 mm in diameter.
Larvae: No information.
Juvenile:  The smallest individuals collected by Provancha and Hall (1991) from the habitats they sampled were 11 mm TL. The smallest individual collected by Gilmore (unpub. data) was 10 mm SL. This may indicate that juveniles settle into benthic habitats at this size.
Adult: Provancha and Hall (1991) consider individuals exceeding 30 mm TL to be adults. Adults reach a maximum size of 75 mm TL (788) with males generally being larger than females (1141; 1214).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Juveniles were found by Carr and Adarns (1973) to consume detritus and copepods. Other studies have found this species to consume copepods, amphipods, mysids, polychaetes. bivalves, chironomid larvae, algae, and other crustaceans (581; 664; 1204). Provancha and Hall (1991) found the diet of Indian River populations to be dominated by a variety of crustaceans (mostly tanaids, amphipods, ostracods, and palaemonid shrimp) and annelids with other items including fishes and unidentified organic matter.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: The clown goby is found commonly in a wide variety of habitats (1141; 887; 848, 1987, 1988; 1242). Odum and Heald (1972) found that Lutjan~ls gt-iseus feeds on this species. A variety of other sparids, sciaenids, lutjanids, flatfish and barracuda, among others, consume various gobiid species (163; 664; 702; 1016; 934; 672; 982). Because of the abundance and consumption by a wide variety of predators, gobies undoubtedly play an important trophic role in most low latitude estuaries.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name: Clown Goby
Scientific Name: Microgobius gulosus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
Class: Osteichthyes
Order: Perciformes
Family: Gobiidae

sections.heading: Other Common Names
sections.content:
Note:	Reference for Scientific Name (Girard 1858)
	Reference for Classification (956)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial: None
Recreational: None
Ecological Role:  The clown goby is found commonly in a wide variety of habitats, including seagrass meadows, mangroves, open bottoms, marsh ponds, canals and fresh water tributaries (1141; 887; 848, 948, 993; 1242). Odum and Heald (1972) found that Lutjanus griseus feeds on this species. A variety of other sparids, sciaenids, lutjanids, flatfish and barracuda, among others, consume various gobiid species (163; 664; 702; 1016; 934; 672; 982). Because of the abundance and consumption by a wide variety of predators, gobies undoubtedly play an important trophic role in most low latitude estuaries.
Indicator: This species has been considered as an indicator of environmental impacts caused by shuttle launches at the Kennedy Space Center (1214). It was chosen for evaluation as an indicator because it occupies the consumer level in the aquatic food web. As such, it would be directly and indirectly affected by chemical and physical changes in the environment, such as ephemeral drops in pH (to 1.5) as a result of shuttle launches (1214).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  The clown goby is found along the Atlantic coast and the Gulf of Mexico from Chesapeake Bay to Colpus Christi, Texas, including Lake Okeechobee, Florida (1116; 632; 1090; 790).
Within Study Area: This goby is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon and its freshwater tributaries (1141; 887; 848, 1987, 1988; 1242; 1187).
Movements and Migrations: This species is a year round resident of shallow fringing habitats within the Indian River Lagoon (Gilmore unpub. data).
Life Mode: The clown goby is a euryhaline, epibenthic, opportunistic carnivore found in a wide variety of habitats, a truly euryoecious species (1086; 887; 848; 790; 1214). This species is sexually dimorphic and displays territorial behavior (1141; 1086).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content: This goby is found in a variety of habitats, including seagrass meadows, mangroves, open bottoms, marsh ponds, canals and fresh water tributaries (1141; 887; 848, 1987. 1988; 1242). Dawson (1969), in work from the Gulf of Mexico, states that "this species occurs most frequently in muddy, estuarine localities and in habitats protected by aquatic vegetation." In the Indian River Lagoon, clown gobies are not found near ocean inlets but are common in quite protected habitats with low hydrological energy (887; 848, 1988; 1098; 1214).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
This species is usually collected over soft sand, silt or muddy bottoms sometimes associated with seagrass, mangroves, or freshwater tributaries (1141, 1116, 848, 1988; 1242; 790; 1214)
Physical/Chemical:  The clown goby has been collected in Florida from waters with a temperature range of 12.0 to 34.1 OC and a salinity range of 0.0 to 36.6 ppt (664; 887; 885).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Clown gobies are gonochoristic, oviparous, and sexual dimorphic. Provancha and Hall (1991) suggest that species with low fecundity such as clown goby may exhibit some parental care. This has been observed in the related species, Gobiosoma bosc by Dahlberg and Conyers (1973), Mok (1981) and others and is typical of gobiid fishes (Breder and Rosen 1966; Thresher 1984).
Mating/Spawning: Provancha and Hall (1991) found that in the northern Indian River Lagoon this goby spawns over a protracted period with young of the year appearing in May. Gonadosomatic index was highest in March and April prior to the onset of spawning. Spawning continued until late fall. Populations from other locations may however spawn all year round as indicated by observations made by Springer and Woodburn (1960). They collected ripe females in July and November in Tampa Bay. Gilmore (unpub. data) has collected individuals less than 15 mm SL from the southern Indian River Lagoon in January, March, May, July, September, October and November.
Fecundity: The mean number of ova was low with 305 + 77.5 eggs found in 25 gravid females from 35 to 49 mm (1214).

sections.heading: GROWTH
sections.content:
Egg: Provancha and Hall (1991) found eggs that were "a dark golden color and well developed" in 4 gravid females (41 to 49 ~nm). These eggs had a total mean diameter of 0.66 + 0.21 mm.  The largest egg examined was 1.14 mm in diameter.
Larvae: No information.
Juvenile:  The smallest individuals collected by Provancha and Hall (1991) from the habitats they sampled were 11 mm TL. The smallest individual collected by Gilmore (unpub. data) was 10 mm SL. This may indicate that juveniles settle into benthic habitats at this size.
Adult: Provancha and Hall (1991) consider individuals exceeding 30 mm TL to be adults. Adults reach a maximum size of 75 mm TL (788) with males generally being larger than females (1141; 1214).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Juveniles were found by Carr and Adarns (1973) to consume detritus and copepods. Other studies have found this species to consume copepods, amphipods, mysids, polychaetes. bivalves, chironomid larvae, algae, and other crustaceans (581; 664; 1204). Provancha and Hall (1991) found the diet of Indian River populations to be dominated by a variety of crustaceans (mostly tanaids, amphipods, ostracods, and palaemonid shrimp) and annelids with other items including fishes and unidentified organic matter.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: The clown goby is found commonly in a wide variety of habitats (1141; 887; 848, 1987, 1988; 1242). Odum and Heald (1972) found that Lutjan~ls gt-iseus feeds on this species. A variety of other sparids, sciaenids, lutjanids, flatfish and barracuda, among others, consume various gobiid species (163; 664; 702; 1016; 934; 672; 982). Because of the abundance and consumption by a wide variety of predators, gobies undoubtedly play an important trophic role in most low latitude estuaries.
